In the face of neoliberal urbanization, cities often become sites of intensified competition for resources, leading to the privatization of public spaces and the marginalization of less affluent communities. This results in a cityscape that caters to the interests of the wealthy and powerful, often at the expense of the poor and disenfranchised. The "right to the city" challenges this dynamic by advocating for a more equitable distribution of urban benefits and a participatory approach to urban governance that includes the voices of all residents, not just the privileged few.

The relationship between "the right to the city" and socio-spatial inequalities is evident in the way urban spaces are organized and who has access to them.
